title: USCIS Revives Public Charge Rule, Allowing Green Card Denials Over Medicaid and Food Stamp Use
excerpt: The Department of Homeland Security has reinstated a Trump-era policy that expands the range of public benefits weighed against green card applicants, effective September 18.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has issued a final rule reviving the "public charge" test for green card applicants, allowing officers to weigh use of Medicaid, food stamps, and housing vouchers in residency decisions.
  • The rule takes effect on September 18, 2026, and USCIS will require a revised Form I-485 for all applications filed on or after that date.
  • The policy reverses a 2022 Biden-era regulation that restricted which benefits could factor into green card determinations, restoring the broader criteria used during Trump's first term.
  • Refugees, asylees, trafficking victims, and petitioners under the Violence Against Women Act remain exempt from the public charge assessment.

The Trump administration on Thursday moved to reinstate sweeping restrictions on immigrants who use public benefits, issuing a final rule that allows federal officers to consider a broad range of government assistance when deciding whether to grant permanent residency.

https://x.com/USCIS/status/2077788228183113863

The Department of Homeland Security published the regulation in the Federal Register on July 16, formally scrapping a 2022 Biden-era policy that had limited which benefits immigration officers could weigh in green card decisions. The rule is scheduled to take effect on September 18.

What the Rule Changes

Under the revived "public charge" framework, USCIS adjudicators can now review an applicant's use of means-tested benefits including Medicaid, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (food stamps), and Section 8 housing vouchers when determining whether the person is likely to become primarily dependent on government assistance.

Officers will also weigh an applicant's age, health, family size, assets, financial resources, education, and skills — a totality-of-the-circumstances approach that mirrors the criteria applied during President Donald Trump's first term.

![The Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg) > **"Federal statute has long required green card applicants to demonstrate they will not become primarily dependent on government benefits."**

"The Trump administration is upholding the rule of law and protecting American taxpayers from subsidizing aliens who may become dependent on public benefits."

— Zach Kahler, USCIS Spokesperson

USCIS will also release a revised Form I-485, the application for adjustment of status. The agency will reject older versions of the form filed on or after September 18, according to the USCIS news release.

A Policy With a Contested History

The concept of a "public charge" test dates back more than a century in U.S. immigration law. Federal statute has long required green card applicants to demonstrate they will not become primarily dependent on government benefits. The dispute centers on how broadly that standard should be applied.

During Trump's first term, the administration adopted a 2019 rule that significantly expanded the definition, counting anyone who received government benefits for more than 12 months in any three-year period as a likely public charge. The policy drew immediate legal challenges and was widely criticized by immigrant advocacy groups who argued it would disproportionately penalize lower-income applicants and deter legal immigrants from accessing benefits they were entitled to.

The Biden administration rescinded the rule in 2022, narrowing the standard to primarily consider only cash welfare payments and long-term government-funded institutional care. The new final rule reverses that approach entirely.

What It Means for Indian Green Card Applicants

![Federal Register — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d6/Cover_of_the_Federal_Register.jpg)

For Indian nationals — who constitute one of the largest groups of employment-based green card applicants — the practical impact depends heavily on individual circumstances. Most Indian green card applicants in employment-based categories hold professional jobs with salaries well above the threshold for public benefits eligibility, which may limit the rule's direct effect on this cohort.

However, immigration attorneys have warned that the rule could create a broader chilling effect. Family-sponsored applicants, dependents who are not working, or individuals who experienced periods of unemployment during their often decade-long green card wait may face additional scrutiny. The rule may also discourage legal immigrants and their family members from accessing benefits they are legally eligible for, even in cases where using those benefits would not disqualify them.

USCIS Director Joseph B. Edlow told CBS News that the agency is "restoring the basic principle that immigrants must be able to support themselves."

Exemptions and Protections

The rule does not apply uniformly. Congress has carved out statutory protections for certain categories of applicants. Refugees, asylees, and individuals granted humanitarian protections — including trafficking victims, certain abuse survivors, and petitioners under the Violence Against Women Act — remain exempt from the public charge determination, according to CBS News.

Benefits collected by an applicant's family members will not be treated as the applicant's own use. However, officers may still consider those benefits when assessing the household's overall ability to support itself, USCIS officials clarified.

Looking Ahead

The rule is expected to affect hundreds of thousands of green card applicants processing within the United States, according to the Washington Examiner. Legal challenges are widely anticipated, given the history of litigation around the 2019 version of the rule.

The 60-day gap before the September 18 effective date gives applicants currently preparing filings a narrow window to submit their I-485 applications under the existing, more lenient framework. Immigration attorneys have advised eligible applicants to file before the deadline where possible.

The policy is the latest in a series of moves by the Trump administration to tighten legal immigration pathways, following recent changes requiring some green card applicants to process from their home countries and the administration's proposal to require bonds of up to $100,000 for certain applicants abroad.
